512.title: Parashurama's challenge
512.hook: on the road home from the wedding, a man with an axe stops Rama: one avatar of Vishnu meets the next
512.carry: avatara: the divine comes down, again and again
512.howItsDone: Hindu tradition counts Parashurama among Vishnu's ten avatars, the Dashavatara, usually listed sixth after the man-lion and the dwarf and before Rama; his birth is marked on Parashurama Jayanti in the spring month of Vaishakha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four couples circled one fire, and Janaka gave Sita to Rama as sahadharmachari, his companion in dharma.

It should be a caravan of pure joy. King Dasharatha, his four sons, four new daughters-in-law, priests, soldiers and wagons of gifts from King Janaka, all rolling back toward Ayodhya. Then the birds begin to cry harshly. At the same moment, deer pass by on the right, a good sign. The king is worried, and Vasishtha reads the signs for him: something frightening is coming, and it will pass. A wind rises. The ground shakes. Dust hides the sun. And out of the dark walks a man with an axe on his shoulder.
screen: `A CARAVAN OF PURE JOY.` → `BAD BIRDS, GOOD DEER.` → `A MAN WITH AN AXE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki describes him like a fire no one can look at straight: matted hair, a bow in one hand, the axe across his shoulder. He's the son of the sage Jamadagni, of the family of Bhrigu, a brahmin, a priest's son, who took up weapons. After his father was killed in a feud with a royal house, the stories say, he made war on the warrior class again and again. Later tradition calls him Parashurama, Rama with the axe. Now he has heard that a young prince broke Shiva's great bow, so he's brought a bow of his own, and a story. Long ago, he says, the divine craftsman made two bows, one for Shiva and one for Vishnu. In his telling, a contest broke out, and one roar from Vishnu left Shiva's bow slack. Shiva's bow passed to the kings of Videha; that's the one Rama broke. Vishnu's bow came down through Parashurama's family, and here it is. String this one, he tells Rama, and then we fight. Dasharatha begs; Parashurama doesn't even answer him. Here is what Hindus see on this road. The word is avatara, a coming down. Hindus count ten great descents of Vishnu, the Dashavatara, and in most lists Parashurama is the sixth and Rama the seventh. Why come down at all? In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, another avatar, gives the reason: whenever dharma falls and wrong rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet. So on a dusty road home from a wedding, one Rama faces another, and in the tradition's eyes, both are Vishnu.

513.title: Rama answers Parashurama
513.hook: Rama strings the bow, spares the sage, and one arrow spends a lifetime of merit
513.carry: punya: merit is real, and it runs out
513.howItsDone: In devotional readings this episode is heard as one avatar of Vishnu meeting the next, and the Bala Kanda as the happy prelude before the Ayodhya Kanda's exile.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parashurama's challenge: an axe on his shoulder, Vishnu's bow in his hand, and one avatar facing the next. Your line was avatara: the divine comes down, again and again.

The king has begged and been ignored. The whole wedding party stands frozen on the road, the brides in their carriages, the soldiers with their hands near their swords. Every eye is on one young man, just married, who has been told to string a god's bow and then fight a warrior who has made kings tremble. You might expect a duel. Valmiki doesn't write one. What Rama does next is quick and quiet, and it ends with nobody hurt.
screen: `THE ROAD STANDS FROZEN.` → `A DUEL? NO.` → `QUICK, QUIET, NOBODY HURT.`

segments.voice: Rama speaks politely and firmly. But you've taken me for someone weak. Watch. He takes the bow out of the sage's hands, strings it, and fits an arrow. Then the surprise. You're a brahmin, Rama says, and related to my teacher Vishvamitra, so I won't loose this at you. But a drawn arrow can't go to waste. It will destroy one of two things: your power to move freely through the world, or the worlds of merit you've won by your austerities. You choose. And the fire goes out of Parashurama. I gave the whole earth away to the sage Kashyapa, he says, and promised not to stay on it at night. Leave me my power to move. Take the worlds I've won. Rama looses the arrow, and those worlds are gone. Here's the Hindu idea underneath. The word is punya, merit: the good that builds up from good deeds and austerity, and it can win a stay in heavenly worlds. But Hindu teaching says those worlds don't last. In the Bhagavad Gita, people who enjoy heaven come back to this world when their merit is used up. Many teachers read this scene that way: merit can be spent in a moment. And then the old warrior does what matters more. He names Rama the undying Lord, walks around him with respect, and leaves for the Mahendra mountain. The first book closes gently: Rama and Sita at home, and Bharata gone to visit his mother's family far away. It matters very soon.

segments.voice: Parashurama walked around Rama with respect, the way Hindus circle a shrine with the holy on their right. If you pray, stand and turn once slowly in place, clockwise, hands together, the way many families end their puja, and offer whatever good you did today without counting it. If you don't pray, stand and turn slowly once anyway, and let one good thing you did today go without keeping score.

514.title: Why the people chose Rama
514.hook: the second book opens with an old king asking a hall full of people: why Rama?
514.carry: Rama is dharma in human form
514.howItsDone: Many Hindu families read the Ayodhya Kanda as the heart of the Ramayana. Rama is often called maryada purushottam, the best of persons who keeps within the bounds of dharma, and his habit of remembering kindness and forgetting wrongs is often held up as a model for children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parashurama's challenge answered: Rama strung the bow, one arrow spent the sage's heavens, and the first book closed at home. Your line was punya: merit is real, and it runs out.

Many people know how the second book of the Ramayana ends: a prince in clothes made of bark, walking into the forest with his wife and his brother. So notice how the Ayodhya Kanda begins. Not with a villain. Not with a quarrel. With an old man who loves his son, and a room full of people who love him too. For the next few weeks, almost everything turns on one family's household, and the first thing in it is good news.
screen: `BARK CLOTHES AND A FOREST: THE END.` → `THE BEGINNING: GOOD NEWS.` → `ONE FAMILY'S HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha has ruled a long time, and he feels it. Rama is the one the whole city talks about. Valmiki pauses to describe him, and one detail stands out. If someone does Rama a single kindness, he is pleased by it. If someone does him a hundred wrongs, he doesn't keep count. So the king makes a plan. He'll name Rama the yuvaraja, the young king, the heir who shares the rule while his father is still alive. He doesn't simply announce it. He calls an assembly: counselors, leading citizens, kings from the lands around, though in his hurry, the text notes, he doesn't send for Janaka or for Bharata's grandfather in Kekaya. If you agree, tell me. If there's a better course, tell me that too. The hall answers with one roar of yes. And the old king tests them: why Rama, while I'm still ruling well? So they tell him. His truthfulness, his courage, his kindness to ordinary people, how he asks after their families and their fields. Here's why this matters to Hindus. Rama is God come down, but the Ramayana keeps showing him as a person you could actually follow. Later in the epic, even an enemy, the demon Maricha, says it plainly: Rama is dharma with a body. That's why grandparents still hold him up to children, and call him maryada purushottam, the best of persons, who keeps within dharma's bounds. Perfect in how he lived it: truthful, kind, a hundred wrongs not counted. And that's why what happens next will hurt so much.

segments.voice: Rama kept one kindness and let a hundred wrongs go uncounted. Bring to mind one kindness someone did for you this year, and let it be vivid: the place, the face. If you pray, offer a quiet thank-you for that person, by name. If a hurt from the same person crowds in, let it sit further back for now, and spend the rest of the sit with the kindness.

515.title: The fast before the crowning
515.hook: the king rushes the crowning to tomorrow, and Rama and Sita spend the night fasting on sacred grass
515.carry: upavasa: a fast is staying near
515.howItsDone: Fasting and keeping vigil the night before a major rite is a common Hindu practice, on days like Ekadashi and Shivaratri and before family pujas; in the text, Dasharatha and then Vasishtha tell Rama and Sita to fast and sleep on kusha grass before the consecration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an old king asked his assembly why Rama, and the hall roared its answer. Your line was Rama is dharma in human form.

Tonight's story has two kinds of waiting in it. One is an old king who can't wait: the assembly has said yes, and now he wants it done by morning. The other is a young couple told how to wait well: a fast, a bath, an offering, and a night on sacred grass before a pouring at dawn. Hindus still keep that second kind of night before a big puja or a holy day. Watch both.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF WAITING.` → `A KING WHO CAN'T WAIT.` → `A COUPLE WHO WAIT WELL.`

segments.voice: First Rama comes to his father's hall, bows, and hears the news in public. Rama goes home. Then the charioteer Sumantra comes back for him: the king wants you again. This time Dasharatha speaks privately, and he sounds afraid. I've had bad dreams. Meteors have fallen with a crash. The astrologers say my star is under pressure from harsh planets. So the coronation will be tomorrow. Then he says something honest, and a little chilling. Do it now, while Bharata is away. Bharata is good, he says, devoted to his elder brother. But the minds of people change, even good people. The king isn't accusing anyone. He's admitting he doesn't trust time. Then he tells Rama what the night requires, and the priest Vasishtha comes to see it done: tonight you and Sita keep a fast, and sleep on the ground, on a bed of sacred kusha grass. Rama and Sita bathe, make an offering, and spend the night quietly in a shrine. Here's the teaching inside that night. The word is upavasa, a fast. Upa means near; vasa, staying. Many teachers read it just that way: a fast isn't a punishment, it's a way of staying near God, setting the plate aside so the mind has room. It's the same spirit in which Hindus still fast on Ekadashi, on Shivaratri, or before a family puja, and it's why a prince sleeps on grass instead of a bed tonight. So two kinds of waiting sit side by side tonight: a couple staying near, and a king who wants it finished before his own son can come home.

segments.voice: Sit the way Rama and Sita sat that night, low and quiet. If you pray, repeat a name you love, Rama, Shiva, or simply om, on each breath out, and let that be the whole sit. If you don't pray, sit with the breath, and when the urge comes to reach for a snack or your phone, let it remind you to come back. That's upavasa, small: staying near instead of filling up.

516.title: The night before the abhisheka
516.hook: a whole city stays up all night getting ready to pour sacred waters over its prince
516.carry: abhisheka: the pouring that honors the holy
516.howItsDone: Abhisheka, the ritual bathing or pouring, is still central to Hindu worship: temple images are bathed with water, milk, honey and other offerings, Shiva lingams especially on Mondays and Shivaratri, and the epic uses the same word for a royal consecration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a fast kept on sacred grass, and a crowning rushed to morning while Bharata was away. Your line was upavasa, a fast is staying near.

The night before a big festival has its own sound. Pots clattering in kitchens past midnight. Ladders against walls. Someone sweeping a street that was already swept. Lights going up in trees. Children who should be asleep, absolutely not asleep. Valmiki gives us Ayodhya on that night, and he takes his time with it. He wants you to see how happy the city is, so you'll feel what it loses by morning.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE A FESTIVAL.` → `LIGHTS IN THE TREES.` → `SO YOU'LL FEEL THE LOSS.`

segments.voice: Start with Rama. Before the night's fast, he goes to his mother Kausalya's rooms, and Lakshmana is there. Rama turns to him and says, in effect: this is yours too. Rule the earth with me. You are my second self. Then the city. Word has spread, and the people of Ayodhya can't keep still. Streets are sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers. Banners go up on the houses. Along the roads they set up lamps like trees of light, so night looks like day. People gather in the squares and talk of nothing else. Meanwhile Vasishtha's helpers gather what the rite will need. The word for the rite is abhisheka, a pouring: the heir is bathed with sacred waters. The text lists what's made ready: gold, white flowers, parched grain, honey and ghee, a white umbrella of state, yak-tail fans, waters from holy rivers. All for a pouring at dawn. Here's where you can still see it. Abhisheka is at the heart of Hindu worship today. In temples, priests bathe the image of the deity with water, milk, honey, curd and ghee, and on Mondays and on Shivaratri, families pour milk and water over the Shiva lingam. Same word, same gesture: you honor what is holy by pouring your best over it, the way a city once honored its prince. And all of Ayodhya's honey and holy water, in a few hours, will sit unused. Valmiki gives this happiness its full weight, so that when it breaks, nothing about it feels small. One person, though, has gone up on a rooftop, and she's looking down at all the lights.

517.title: Manthara on the rooftop
517.hook: a maid on a rooftop sees the lights, and the first person she tells is overjoyed for a son not her own
517.carry: sama-darshana: seeing everyone with equal eyes
517.howItsDone: Manthara's name is sometimes used for someone who stirs up trouble in a family, but the Ayodhya Kanda is read closely enough that Kaikeyi's first, generous reaction is often pointed out.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a city lit for a pouring at dawn, the same abhisheka temples still offer. Your line was abhisheka, the pouring that honors the holy.

Valmiki doesn't tell us much about where she came from. She's a maid from Queen Kaikeyi's family household, and she has always lived beside Kaikeyi. Her name is Manthara. The text says her back is bent. On the night before the coronation, she happens to climb up to a high terrace, the way anyone might go up to the roof to see what the noise is about. And below her, the whole city is glowing.
screen: `A MAID FROM KAIKEYI'S FAMILY.` → `UP TO THE ROOF.` → `THE CITY IS GLOWING.`

segments.voice: Manthara sees banners, flowers, people in their best clothes, music in the streets. What's going on, she asks a nurse nearby. Why is Kausalya, Rama's mother, handing out gifts? The nurse, delighted, tells her: tomorrow the king will make Rama his heir. Manthara goes down the stairs in a fury. She finds Kaikeyi lying on her bed. Get up, she says. Something terrible is happening to you. The king is going to make Rama heir. Your good fortune is about to dry up like a river in summer. And here is the first surprise. Kaikeyi is glad. Truly glad. She sits up and gives Manthara a beautiful jewel as a reward for the news. Then she says the line that matters most. Rama and Bharata are the same to me. I see no difference between them. Hindus have a name for that kind of seeing: sama-darshana, equal vision. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the wise look with the same eyes on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person the world shuns, because the same Self lives in all of them. Tonight, Kaikeyi has that vision for two boys, her own son and another woman's. Quick retellings make her the wicked stepmother from her first scene. Valmiki doesn't. He shows her generous first, so that when she changes, you watch equal eyes go narrow. Manthara has heard all this. And she throws the jewel on the floor.

segments.voice: Picture two people side by side: one you find easy to love, and one you don't. If you pray, say a blessing for both in the same breath; many Hindus close their prayers with sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy. If you don't pray, simply wish them both well, the same wish, on each breath out, and notice where the wish wants to be smaller for one of them.

518.title: Manthara's whisper
518.hook: how a whisper works: not one big lie, but a picture of the future, told over and over
518.carry: satsang: the company you keep shapes the mind
518.howItsDone: In Ramlila and in homes where the Ramcharitmanas is read, the goddess Sarasvati turns Manthara's mind at the gods' request; readers of Valmiki often note that his telling leaves the motive human.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Manthara on the rooftop, and Kaikeyi, glad, seeing no difference between Rama and her son. Your line was sama-darshana, seeing everyone with equal eyes.

Someone takes you aside. They're not angry at you; they're worried for you. Haven't you noticed, they say, how things are going to go? And they paint you a picture of next year, and in it you're smaller, and someone else is laughing. Nothing they've said is quite a lie. But by the end, people you loved an hour ago look different. That's what happens in Kaikeyi's room tonight, and it's why Hindu teachers care so much about whose voice you sit with.
screen: `TAKEN ASIDE.` → `A PICTURE OF NEXT YEAR.` → `NOTHING QUITE A LIE.`

segments.voice: Manthara throws away the jewel and starts building the picture. Once Rama is king, she says, his son will be king after him, and Bharata will be cut out of the line forever. Worse, a king fears his brothers: Rama will send Bharata away, or have him killed. And you, she tells Kaikeyi, were the king's favorite. Now Kausalya will be queen mother, and you'll stand in her hall like a servant. Kaikeyi pushes back at first. Rama is the eldest, she says. He's good, he's truthful, he treats me like his own mother. She doesn't fall at the first push. But Manthara keeps going, the picture gets sharper, and slowly Kaikeyi's face changes. By the end she's asking: how do we stop this? Why did Manthara do it? Valmiki gives her loyalty to Kaikeyi and Bharata, and plenty of bitterness. Later retellings, like Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, add that the gods asked the goddess Sarasvati to turn her mind, so Rama would go to the forest and, in time, defeat Ravana. Either way, many Hindu teachers read this scene as a lesson about company. The word is sanga. Satsang is the company of the true and the good; kusang is bad company. It's part of why families gather to sing bhajans together, why a grandmother wants you at the temple: the mind takes the color of what it keeps hearing. Kaikeyi, who had equal eyes an hour ago, turned in one night with the wrong voice in her ear.
screen: `MANTHARA PAINTS THE FUTURE.` · `KAIKEYI PUSHES BACK.` · `HOW DO WE STOP THIS?` · `SATSANG AND KUSANG.` · then, large: `THE MIND TAKES THE COLOR OF ITS COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Think of a picture of the future someone handed you lately, about you or about another person, and notice whose voice it's in. Then put a better voice beside it.
